summary: RFC 6598 says reverse DNS queries for Shared Address Space, 100.64.0.0/10, must not go to the global DNS. This best current practice directs IANA to add the matching zones to the IPv4 Locally-Served DNS Zones registry so such queries do not leak out.

eli5.summary: Some addresses are only for private use. This makes sure questions about their names are answered locally and never sent out to the world.

questions: why is reverse dns for 100.64.0.0/10 important
what zones are in the locally-served dns registry
subtitle: Keeping private reverse DNS queries out of the global system.

tldr.problem: Reverse DNS queries for Shared Address Space (100.64.0.0/10) were sometimes being forwarded to the global DNS system, which is incorrect for private addresses.
tldr.mechanism: This document directs IANA to add the corresponding reverse-DNS zones to the IPv4 Locally-Served DNS Zones Registry, telling recursive nameservers to handle these queries locally instead.
tldr.outcome: DNS servers now treat Shared Address Space reverse queries the same way they treat private address reverse queries, preventing them from leaking out.

today: RFC 7793 is a Best Current Practice and remains the definitive guidance on handling reverse DNS for Shared Address Space.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Shared Address Space is a special range of IPv4 addresses (100.64.0.0/10) reserved for use within networks that may be seen by other parties. It differs from private addresses like 192.168.0.0/16, which are never expected to appear on the public internet.

RFC 6598 specifies that reverse DNS queries for these Shared Address Space addresses MUST NOT be forwarded to the global DNS system. This document formalizes that requirement by adding the corresponding zones to IANA's IPv4 Locally-Served DNS Zones Registry. This registry tells recursive nameservers which zones they should answer locally without asking the global DNS infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are for private use only. This makes sure that when someone asks "who owns this private address?", the answer comes from your local DNS, not from the internet.

sections.title: What is Shared Address Space
sections.content:
RFC 6598 defined Shared Address Space as a special allocation for Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) scenarios. These are addresses used by service providers when they need to translate between subscriber networks and the internet. Unlike traditional private addresses that only appear within a single organization, Shared Address Space addresses can be seen by both the subscriber and the service provider.

Because Shared Address Space addresses can appear on both sides of a network boundary, they must be treated with care. Reverse DNS queries (asking "what hostname is associated with this IP?") must never reach the global DNS system for these addresses, just as they must not for private addresses like 10.0.0.0/8.
sections.eli5: Shared Address Space is like a party invite list that both the organizer and the guests use. Unlike your personal address book, it can be visible to multiple people, but it still should not leak to strangers.

sections.title: The Shared Address Space Range
sections.content: Shared Address Space covers the IPv4 block 100.64.0.0/10, which includes all addresses from 100.64.0.0 to 100.127.255.255. In reverse DNS, addresses are looked up by constructing domain names in the IN-ADDR.ARPA zone. The 100.0.0.0/8 block maps to zones named 64.100.IN-ADDR.ARPA through 127.100.IN-ADDR.ARPA (64 through 127 because those are the second octets in 100.64 through 100.127).
sections.eli5: All those special addresses live in zones with names like 64.100.IN-ADDR.ARPA. These are the "mailboxes" where reverse DNS questions about these addresses are answered.

sections.title: Changes to the Registry
sections.content:
This document directs IANA to add 64 DNS zones to the IPv4 Locally-Served DNS Zones Registry (established by RFC 6303). These zones are: 64.100.IN-ADDR.ARPA through 127.100.IN-ADDR.ARPA. Each zone corresponds to one /8 subdivision within the Shared Address Space block.

When a recursive nameserver receives a reverse DNS query for an address in this range, it will consult the registry and handle the query locally instead of forwarding it. The RFC also notes that DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) requires that the delegation chain be broken for these zones to prevent validation failures.
sections.eli5: The registry is updated with a list of 64 local zones. DNS servers check the registry and say "I will answer this locally" instead of asking the internet.

sections.title: Security Impact
sections.content: This document adds no new security risks to the internet. It simply extends an existing practice (established in RFC 6303 for private addresses) to Shared Address Space addresses. By preventing queries from leaking to the global DNS, it actually improves security by preventing information disclosure about private network topology and reducing unnecessary DNS traffic.
sections.eli5: This change does not create new dangers. It actually prevents a potential problem by keeping questions about private addresses from escaping to the internet.
